Vignette: Nadia, Age 44

Nadia grew up believing that the law could hold the world together. She spent her childhood in Beirut watching her father, a civil court judge, press his robes each morning with the same quiet conviction - that order was possible, that justice was real. She carried that belief with her to law school, through her marriage to a gentle architect named Tariq, and into her career as a prosecutor in a mid-sized American city, where she has spent fifteen years building cases against people who hurt other people. She is good at it. She is precise, methodical, and patient in ways that younger colleagues admire and occasionally find unsettling.

Four years ago, Nadia flew back to Lebanon to visit her mother and two sisters during what everyone hoped would be a calm summer. It was not calm. The neighborhood where she grew up was struck during a period of renewed shelling. She was inside her mother's apartment on the third afternoon when the building across the street took a direct hit. The windows shattered inward. Her younger sister, Rana, was cut badly by the glass. Nadia pressed a folded tablecloth against Rana's arm for forty minutes, crouched behind the kitchen counter, listening to sounds she cannot name even now - not the explosion itself, which she barely registered in the moment, but what came after. The crying from the street. The particular silence between sounds. The smell of something burning that she later understood was the apartment where a family she had known since childhood had been living.

Rana recovered. Nadia flew home to Tariq two weeks later and told him she was fine, that Rana was fine, that these things happened. She went back to work within days.

The first sign that something was wrong came in the courtroom. Nadia was presenting evidence in an arson case - photographs of a burned interior, the smell of accelerant still faintly embedded in the exhibit bags - and she lost her place entirely. She stood at the podium for what felt like a very long time. She found her notes again and finished, and no one seemed to notice, but she noticed. She began avoiding cases that involved fire, then cases involving structural damage, then, more quietly, cases where photographs showed destroyed rooms of any kind. She reroutes this without fully acknowledging it, assigning those files to junior prosecutors and offering administrative rationales that are not untrue, exactly, but are not the real reason.

At home she sleeps poorly. She wakes between two and four in the morning and lies still, listening to the house. Tariq has learned not to ask too many questions, though she can see the concern he carries carefully around her. She finds herself checking the locks twice before bed, and then again. When a truck backfires on the street outside the courthouse, her body responds before her mind does - a flooding, physical alarm that embarrasses her deeply and that she believes she hides well. She does not hide it as well as she thinks.

She has not told her mother what the weeks after the shelling cost her. Her mother lived through the civil war and does not, in Nadia's estimation, have the luxury of hearing about Nadia's difficulty sleeping. This is how she frames it to herself - as a question of proportion, of who has the right to struggle. She holds herself to a standard of functionality that is, in many ways, genuinely impressive. She still wins cases. She still makes Tariq laugh at dinner. She still calls her sisters every Sunday.

But there is a part of her daily life that has quietly contracted. She no longer walks past construction sites if she can help it. She has not been back to Lebanon. She has begun to understand, in the slow and reluctant way that intelligent people sometimes come to difficult truths, that what happened in her mother's kitchen did not stay in her mother's kitchen - that it followed her home and has been living there ever since, rearranging things while she was at work.
